1.pericope_label: Solomon confirmed king over all Israel, and the roll of the great officers of his court

schools.summary: Henry reads the opening notice as confirmation and establishment over all Israel, not as with his successors over two tribes only, and adds that he was a king in the sense that he did the work and duty of one with the wisdom God had given him, since those preserve the honour of a place who mind its business. On the officers he makes the continuity the lesson: several are the same who served in his father’s time, Zadok and Abiathar as priests, Jehoshaphat as recorder, Benaiah in military affairs, and the sons of his father’s scribe as his own; Solomon, though a wise man, would not affect to be wiser than his father in the matter. When sons come to inherit their father’s wealth, honour and power it is a piece of respect to his memory, where it can properly be done, to employ whom he employed and trust whom he trusted, whereas many pride themselves on being the reverse of their good parents. He notes further that the rest were priests’ sons, the prime minister being a son of Zadok and two others sons of Nathan the prophet, in preferring whom the king testified the grateful respect he had for their good father, whom he loved in the name of a prophet.

Gill draws the contrast at both ends of the history, since David was not at first king over all Israel but only over Judah, and Solomon’s successors were not after the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam; and he connects the notice to the wisdom recounted in the preceding chapter, so that Solomon reigned by the consent of all and in the hearts of all the people. He glosses the princes simply as those in office about the king, in the highest posts of honour and trust. On the scribes he observes that their father had been scribe only in David’s time and, being very probably dead, both his sons were continued in the office as secretaries of state, Solomon having more business for such an office than his father had.

Ellicott finds the weight laid on the word all characteristic of a writer compiling the book after the disruption of the kingdom. He divides the officers into those attached to the court and those invested with local authority, derives the word for princes from a root meaning to set in order, and notes it as significant that whereas in the two lists of David’s officers the captain of the host stands first, here both military offices are preceded by the peaceful offices of priest, scribes and recorder. On the title given to Azariah he concedes the wider usage of the word, which keeps traces of the old time when priesthood and the headship of a family were united and so was applied to princes, being given to the sons of David where the parallel in Chronicles paraphrases it as chief about the king, and he notes that David himself on occasion wore the priestly ephod; but here, he holds, there is every reason for the usual priestly sense, Azariah having been a prince before he succeeded to the high priesthood, and the mingling of priestly and princely functions being characteristic of the time. He adds that Chronicles makes Azariah the son of Ahimaaz and so Zadok’s grandson, that the title must be given here by anticipation since the text says a little below that Zadok and Abiathar were the priests, and that Abiathar, though disgraced and practically deposed, was still regarded theoretically as priest, the priesthood being properly for life, much as Annas is called high priest in the Gospels. He identifies the scribe’s office as that of a secretary of state issuing the king’s edicts and letters, the recorder as the annalist who drew up and preserved the archives, and takes the father of Zabud for Nathan the son of David, since the title in question is ascribed to David’s sons and Nathan the prophet always has his title appended wherever he is first named in this book. Keil and Delitzsch go the other way on the chief point: the word applied to Azariah is not the priest at all but the administrator of the kingdom, the representative of the king before the people, the article marking him the one who held first place among the confidential counsellors; and they reject the construal of the Vulgate, Luther and Thenius which, against the accents, joins the word genitivally to the patronymic. They observe that the first of the princes is not the commander-in-chief, as under the warlike reign of David, but, suiting Solomon’s peaceful rule, the administrator of the kingdom; they date the list to the middle of the reign, since two of the officers married daughters of Solomon, which they could not have done till his later years; they accept Theodoret’s as the only possible explanation of Abiathar’s being named, that Solomon deprived him of the office but not of the priestly dignity, which was hereditary; they deny Thenius’s view that Nathan the prophet is meant and take the father of Azariah and Zabud for David’s son of that name, which makes both men nephews of Solomon; and they note the office of governor of the palace as one met with for the first time under Solomon.

Clarke remarks that these men were the king’s great, chief or principal men and that none of them were princes in the common acceptation of the word. He glosses the offices for a modern reader, the scribes as secretaries to the king, the recorder as historiographer who chronicled the affairs of the kingdom, Zabud as perhaps what we should call premier or prime minister, and the king’s friend as his chief favourite and confidant.

positions.view: Not the priesthood at all, but the administrator of the kingdom and the king’s representative before the people
The usual priestly sense here, though the word was elsewhere applied to princes; he was a prince before succeeding to the high priesthood

debates.question: Why is Abiathar named as priest when Solomon had deposed him?

positions.view: With Theodoret, he was stripped of the office but not of the priestly dignity, which was hereditary
He was still regarded theoretically as priest, the priesthood being properly for life, as Annas is called high priest in the Gospels

debates.question: Which Nathan was the father of Azariah and Zabud?

positions.view: Not the prophet, against Thenius, but David’s son of that name, making both men Solomon’s nephews
David’s son, since the prophet always has his title appended where first named in this book

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the officer list into a lesson on inherited service, that it is a piece of respect to a father’s memory to employ whom he employed.
Alone in insisting that none of these men were princes in the common acceptation of the word.

7.pericope_label: The twelve officers and their districts, each providing for the king’s household a month in the year

schools.summary: Henry explains the purpose of the arrangement under four heads: that the king’s house might always be well furnished at the best hand, great men learning from it to be generous in spending according to their ability but prudent in providing; that the king and his immediate attendants might be eased of care and apply themselves the more closely to the business of the state; that all parts of the kingdom might be equally benefited by the taking off of their own productions and the circulating of the coin, so that industry was encouraged and wealth increased even in the tribes most remote from the court; and that dividing the trust into so many hands kept any one man from being continually burdened with the care or growing exorbitantly rich with the profit of it, while giving the king men in every district who, having a dependence on the court, would be serviceable to his interest. He notes that several are named only by their surnames, as great men commonly call their servants, that two of them married Solomon’s daughters and that it was no disparagement to the daughters to marry men of business, a better match with Israelite officers of their father’s court than with sons of princes who were strangers to the covenant of promise; and he resolves the apparent contradiction about the one officer in that land by making the other two subordinate to him.

Gill explains the number as answering not to the twelve tribes, since it does not appear that each officer had a whole tribe under him but only particular places within a tribe, but to the twelve months of the year, in which each took his turn. He supposes the fathers’ names to be given in place of the officers’ own because the fathers were well known. He adds conjectures of his own as the list proceeds: that the district beyond Jordan must have been very fruitful, since one officer furnished the king’s provision for a month from it; that Asher was a very plentiful tribe, particularly for oil; that one officer was perhaps the son of Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, and promoted for his father’s sake; and that another is described by his father’s name to distinguish him from the Shimei who cursed David, who was of the same tribe. He resolves the difficulty at Gilead as Henry does, by excepting what lay under the other officer’s jurisdiction.

Keil and Delitzsch deny that these officers were chamberlains or administrators of the royal domains, as Michaelis and Ewald held, since officers of that kind appear in Chronicles under a different title; they are rather chief tax-collectors, in Rosenmüller’s phrase general receivers of taxes, levying the king’s duties, which in the East consisted then as now mostly of the produce of the land rather than of money payments as in the West, and delivering them at the royal kitchen. They add that Josephus’s rendering of the term by governors and generals cannot be used, as Thenius uses it, to infer that they exercised a kind of government, that explanation being merely a subjective conjecture. On the five patronymics they think it very improbable that proper names dropped out five times, as Clericus and Michaelis supposed, and are left with the assumption that the men bore their fathers’ names with the prefix as their own, on the analogy of a similar name in Chronicles, conceding that one of the five looks very strange so taken. They identify the officer of Dor as probably a son of David’s elder brother and so Solomon’s cousin as well as his son-in-law, and another as most likely a brother of the chancellor; and they charge the Septuagint with arbitrarily interpolating a word before one place-name, which Thenius naturally takes under his protection without considering that it yields no sense unless another word precedes it. Ellicott agrees that the office denotes the collection of revenue, mostly in kind, for the court, household and guards, but allows it may have included the management of the royal domain lands as well. He calls the five patronymics curious and lays them to some defect in the archives from which the chapter is evidently drawn, infers from the two royal marriages that the office must have been one of high importance and dignity, and counts the provinces as nine west and three east of Jordan, finding that they coincide only in a few cases with the lands assigned to the tribes — from which he thinks much of the tribal division had by this time probably become obsolete, though Chronicles shows it still in force for chieftainship over men and for the levy in war. He identifies the districts city by city and settles one name by stating which form is the right reading.

Clarke observes only that the business of the twelve was to provide daily, each for a month, the provisions consumed in the king’s household, and that the task of such a daily provision was no easy one.

positions.view: Chief tax-collectors, levying the king’s duties in kind; not administrators of the royal domains, against Michaelis and Ewald
Collectors of revenue, mostly in kind, which may also have included management of the royal domain lands
Providers of the daily household provision, each for his month

debates.question: Why are five of the twelve given by patronymic only?

positions.view: They bore their fathers’ names with the prefix as their own proper names; it is improbable that names dropped out five times
Some defect in the archives from which the chapter is drawn
The fathers’ names were given because the fathers were well known
They are named by their surnames, as great men commonly call their servants

debates.question: Do the twelve districts answer to the old tribal allotments?

positions.view: Only in a few cases; much of the tribal division had probably become obsolete, though still in force for chieftainship and the war levy
No; each officer held particular places within a tribe, the number answering to the months and not the tribes

Alone in conjecturing that one of the officers was a son of Hushai the Archite and promoted for his father’s sake.

20.pericope_label: Judah and Israel numerous and at peace, the daily provision of the court, and the extent of the dominion

schools.summary: Henry takes the whole description as a type of the Messiah’s kingdom, answering the prophecies of the seventy-second Psalm, and works it out in order: the territories large and the tributaries many, so that princes added to the king’s honour by homage and to his wealth by presents, while he gave them instructions in return, wisdom being better than gold; the subjects numerous, so that the promise to Abraham concerning the increase of his seed was fulfilled along with that concerning the extent of their dominion; and the people easy, dwelling with confidence, not jealous of their king or his officers nor in fear of enemies foreign or domestic. He makes a point of the property: Solomon invaded no man’s, and took not their vineyards and oliveyards to himself as had been the manner of the king, so that what men had they could call their own, and the peace was such that they might dwell as safely under the shadow of a vine as within the walls of a city. On the court he reckons the flour and meal would richly serve three thousand men, and reports Carellus at above four thousand eight hundred; he observes that the king kept not a table of dainties or deceitful meats, against which he himself witnessed, but substantial food for those who came to hear his wisdom. On the horses he sets the forty thousand for chariots and twelve thousand for the troops beside the commandment that the king should not multiply horses, and argues that considering the extent and wealth of the kingdom Solomon did not multiply them in proportion to his neighbours, since the Philistines had once brought thirty thousand chariots into the field and the Syrians at least forty thousand horse. He notes that the same officers who provided for the house provided for the stable, every man knowing his place and work and time, so that a great court was kept without confusion, and closes on the preacher’s text, that when goods increase those are increased that eat them.

Gill assigns causes for the multitude, great fruitfulness in their families with neither pestilential disease nor wars to lessen their number, so that the promise to Abraham was fulfilled; and he reads both the multitude and the safe dwelling as emblems of Christ’s spiritual subjects, especially in the latter day, Solomon being a type of him. He glosses the dominion as extending over all the people round about, who stood in fear of him, or brought him presents and paid tribute as an acknowledgment of superiority. He measures the vessel of the daily provision at Bishop Cumberland’s seventy-five wine gallons and five pints and somewhat more, by which the quantity of fine flour consumed in one day may be known, and explains that the dominion beyond the river accounts for the plenty of provisions and the revenue with which such a table was supported.

Keil and Delitzsch read the numbering as the sand of the sea as showing that the promise given to the patriarchs had been fulfilled, and the extent of the rule as showing the other part of it fulfilled too, that the seed should possess the gates of its enemies; they note the missing copula at the head of the verse and that the Septuagint, Vulgate and Luther therefore connect the first fourteen verses of the next chapter with this one. They explain the phrase rendered on this side the river as meaning the land west of the Euphrates, the usage arising because the author of the books was living in exile on the other side of it and describes the extent of the kingdom taking that as his starting-point. They calculate the daily consumption from Thenius’s value for the measure, so that ninety of them would yield some twenty-eight thousand pounds of bread, and at two pounds a head put fourteen thousand persons at Solomon’s court, with a consumption of flesh quite in proportion. They add a textual caution, that most commentators supply a missing preposition before the land of the Philistines from the parallel in Chronicles, but that it is improbable so indispensable a word dropped out and unnecessary to supply it, since the preposition of the preceding clause may be repeated in thought. Ellicott presses the description further than mere prosperity: it specifies that Israel were now a dominant race, relieved of all burden of labour and ruling over subject peoples reduced to complete subjection and serfship, and that now for the first time they entered full possession of the territory promised at the Conquest — it was otherwise afterwards, as the complaints brought to Rehoboam show. On the empire he is careful about what the dominion was: as in all ancient Eastern empires it represented not an organised monarchy but the supremacy of a dominant kingdom over tributaries gathered round, so that it would rise rapidly and as rapidly fall to pieces; it was the fruit of the warlike energy of the two preceding reigns but was sustained less by military power than by the peaceful forces of wealth and policy, and was largely dependent on Solomon’s personal ascendancy; and he holds the Syrian kingdoms, like Tyre, to have been allies on a footing of some dependence rather than tributaries proper. He agrees that the phrase about the river means literally the further side reckoned from Babylon, and draws from it that the book was composed at the time of the Exile or at least when the Babylonish empire so governed the nomenclature of the East. On the measure he allows it is variously estimated between forty-two and eighty-six gallons and will say only that the quantity indicates probably several thousands in the household, court and guard, and he takes the game named as wild game distinct from the herds and flocks, the fatted fowl apparently signifying dainty food generally.

Clarke alone reads the eating and drinking and making merry against the grain: they were very comfortable, very rich, very merry and very corrupt, and this full feeding and dissipation led to a total corruption of manners. He maps the dominion from the Euphrates east to the Philistines west on the Mediterranean and Egypt south, infers Syria, Damascus, Moab and Ammon as tributaries lying between, and concludes with Calmet that Solomon appears to have possessed all the land God covenanted with Abraham to give his posterity. He itemises the daily provision and works through the names of the game philologically, taking the first word to comprehend both sheep and goats, the next as the deer, the next as the gazelle or antelope, and the next as the buffalo; of the fatted fowl he supposes it means all the wild fowls in season during each month, reports Michaelis deriving the word from a root signifying field or desert, so that it may signify creatures living in fields, woods and deserts taken by hunting as opposed to the domesticated, and consequently may include beasts as well as fowls, and asks of those who have translated it capons whether any such thing was known among the ancient Jews. He reports the two highest estimates of the court, Vilalpandus at not less than forty-eight thousand six hundred and Calvisius at fifty-four thousand, and accounts for them by supposing the guards included, each receiving a ration from the king’s store.

positions.view: About three thousand, or above four thousand eight hundred on Carellus’s reckoning
Probably several thousands in the household, court and guard
Fourteen thousand, calculated from Thenius’s value for the measure at two pounds of bread a head
Vilalpandus at not less than forty-eight thousand six hundred, Calvisius at fifty-four thousand, the guards included

debates.question: What were the fatted fowl of the daily provision?

positions.view: Perhaps all the wild fowls in season each month; with Michaelis, creatures of field and desert taken by hunting, which may include beasts as well as fowls — and not capons, unknown among the ancient Jews

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the national festivity as moral decline, and alone in working the names of the game through philologically to ask whether capons were known among the ancient Jews.
Alone in characterising the empire as the supremacy of a dominant kingdom over gathered tributaries, which would rise and fall rapidly and rested on personal ascendancy rather than military power.
Alone in defending Solomon against the commandment not to multiply horses, by comparison with the far greater cavalry of the Philistines and Syrians.

29.pericope_label: The gift of wisdom and largeness of heart, the three thousand proverbs and the thousand and five songs

schools.summary: Henry holds Solomon’s wisdom to have been more his glory than his wealth, and traces it to its fountain, that God gives the powers of reason, preserves and improves them, their ordinary advance being owing to his providence and their sanctification to his grace, while this extraordinary pitch was a special grant in answer to prayer. He offers three readings of largeness of heart in turn: the intellectual powers, the heart being often put for those; or courage and boldness and the assurance with which he delivered his determinations; or a disposition to do good with knowledge, being free and communicative, as free of his learning as he was of his meat, and grudging it to none about him. On the comparison he says that if nature excels art, much more does grace, the knowledge God gives by special favour going beyond what man gets by his own labour. He takes the four rivals for the Levites whom David employed in the temple music, notes that one of them was the king’s seer in the word of God and that two were own brothers, and holds it uncertain whether the proverbs we now have were any part of the three thousand at all; of the songs he allows one only extant, because that only was divinely inspired. He makes Solomon a moralist in the proverbs, a poet in the songs, and a natural philosopher in what he wrote of plants and animals, some thinking of their medicinal use; and he calls the court the staple of learning and the rendezvous of philosophers, who came to light their candle at his lamp.

Gill insists the wisdom came neither from the acuteness of Solomon’s genius nor from his industry and diligence but by the gift of God, the fountain of whatever solid wisdom and understanding is in any man, and describes it as reaching things natural, moral, divine and spiritual, not slight and superficial but exceeding deep and large beyond expression. He places the wisdom of the children of the east in the knowledge of the stars, divination by birds and soothsaying, naming the Arabians and Persians. He takes the claim that Solomon was wiser than all men to hold not only of those living in his time but of ages past since the fall of Adam and of times to come, especially in natural knowledge in all its branches, since though some men excel in some part of knowledge none excelled in all as he did. He accounts for the loss of the proverbs: they were not written as the book of Proverbs was but spoken only, taken from his lips and spread by those who heard them for the use of others, and in process of time lost, whereas the book, being written under divine inspiration, is preserved.

Ellicott separates the three terms carefully: understanding is high intellectual power and largeness of heart is capacity of knowledge, and both are distinguished from the higher gift of wisdom to which they are only means, the one being the capacity of wisdom within and the other the education of that capacity from without. He then gives an account of wisdom as properly an attribute of God reflected in man by revelation, so that the wisdom of man is the knowledge of the true end of his own being, a vain search in Ecclesiastes and embodied as found in Proverbs, with the fear of the Lord as its beginning and faith as the supplement of its necessary imperfection; and he turns the gift into a warning, that if the sense of the need of revelation be lost this very consciousness of wisdom may become a self-idolatry in which the mind prides itself on having pierced to the secret of being, holds that such knowledge sets it above ordinary law and duty, and delights in philosophical contemplation rather than in active energy and religious devotion. On the rival wisdoms he makes the children of the east morally serious, Job being expressly one of them and among the chief, so that what their wisdom was the utterances of Job and his friends testify, showing large knowledge of nature and of man and resting, with an awe greater than was felt within the Abrahamic covenant, on the consciousness of the one God; Egyptian wisdom he takes for part of a more advanced and elaborate civilisation, enriched by learning and manifest in art and science but perhaps less free and vigorous than the simpler patriarchal wisdom of the east. On the four rivals he grants the coincidence with the genealogy in Chronicles remarkable enough to suggest identification and then refuses it, since the passage implies rivals contemporary with Solomon rather than a family generations earlier, and identifies them instead with the Heman and Ethan whom David set over the service of song, noting that the patronymic of the other two signifies dance or music and may be no name at all. He derives the word for proverb from a root signifying comparison, distinguishes four senses of it, and observes that the collected series fall far short of the number given in the text. Keil and Delitzsch take the children of the east primarily for the Arabian tribes celebrated for gnomic wisdom, the Sabaeans and Temanites among them, and hold that the governing word requires the Chaldaeans too, celebrated for astronomy and astrology. They identify the four rivals with the sons of Zerach in Chronicles, the names agreeing but one, whose difference they lay to a copyist’s error, and support it from the title Ezrahite borne by two of them in the Psalms, derived from the family name lengthened by a prosthetic letter, while conceding that both men were Levites. Of the writings they call what survives in the book of Proverbs a comparatively small portion and probably a selection of the best, and allow besides the Song of Songs two psalms which bear Solomon’s name and justly bear it; and they set the cedar against the hyssop as the largest and the smallest growths, so as to embrace the whole vegetable kingdom.

Clarke says God gave Solomon a capacious mind and furnished him with extraordinary assistance to cultivate it, and is content with Lord Bacon’s figure, which he calls happy and correct, that as the sand on the sea-shore encloses a great body of waters so Solomon’s mind contained an ocean of knowledge. He names the children of the east as the Chaldeans, Persians and Arabians, who with the Egyptians were famed for wisdom through all the world. On the four rivals he denies that the four of the same names in Chronicles are probably the same persons, since they are there called sons of Zerah and he flourished long before Solomon’s time, and reports the suggestion that the patronymic of two should be rendered masters of dancing or music, the word signifying a choir and also a pipe instrument, so that the comparison may refer to Solomon’s skill in music and poetry. He counts the surviving proverbs at about nine hundred, or no more than six hundred and fifty if the first nine chapters are not Solomon’s, and of the thousand and five songs allows only one remaining, holding that the psalm sometimes added appears more properly a psalm of direction left him by his father concerning the building of the temple.
